Consumers trust that when regulators allow chemicals in products like food packaging, it’s because it’s been through safety testing, Muncke said. “But that’s not the case,” she said. “And it doesn’t make sense.” The team has done a “very, very good job” highlighting how little is known about the risks of substances that affect everyone, said Maricel Maffini, an independent chemical safety and regulation expert who was not involved in the study but has collaborated with Muncke in the past. Because the study focused on a list that people in industry and regulators regard as reliable, it’s looking under the proverbial lamppost, Maffini said. While there’s plenty of information suggesting that many of these chemicals should not be on the market or should have stronger regulations, she said, there’s so much information beyond that list that’s missing. In previous work, Muncke and her team identified more than 15,000 chemicals used in food processing or packaging from lists of substances approved by regulators in the United States, China, Japan, and countries in Europe and South America or that had been identified in studies . In the new paper, they analyzed that “jaw-dropping” number of chemicals, Muncke said, to flag the most problematic. To maximize the utility of their priority list, the team used only data obtained from governmental and regulatory agencies linking a chemical to human health hazards such as cancer, reproductive harm, or ability to concentrate in the body. That yielded a priority list of 1,222 chemicals that they ranked into four tiers, with the highest to lowest evidence of human exposure from food-contact materials. Ninety-four chemicals known to seep into food and detected in breast milk, blood, or other human samples were assigned to Tier 1, the highest priority for regulators and companies to consider phasing out. These chemicals include liver- and immune system-damaging PFAS “forever chemicals,” which make food wrappers grease- or water-resistant; the likely carcinogen styrene , used to produce takeout packages and refrigerated dairy food containers; hormone-disrupting phthalates , added to make plastics like those that hold vegetable oils flexible; and bisphenol A, added to hard plastics and can linings and a poster child for endocrine disruptors’ ability to impair development at low doses. Studies have found these and other chemicals leaching from containers into a diverse array of food and beverages, including water, infant formula , orange juice , ice cream , yogurt and cream , oils, cake, and fatty foods . The next highest priority list, Tier 2, included an additional 264 hazardous chemicals that leach into food but have not been detected in biomonitoring studies. At least, not yet. Experts with the Food Packaging Forum say regulators can take simple steps to reduce people’s exposure to harmful chemicals found or used in food-contact materials, starting with moving away from evaluating one chemical at a time. People are exposed to multiple synthetic chemicals simultaneously through food-contact materials, textiles, personal-care products, air pollution, and more. Regulators should introduce a “mixture allocation factor,” which creates a safety margin that accounts for the combined effects of multiple chemicals in a single exposure. Chemicals should be regulated in groups. If there is sufficient evidence that individual chemicals in a group with similar structures and properties are hazardous, then all members of that group should be pulled from the market or not approved until proven safe, as the European Union did in its 2023 proposal to restrict PFAS as a group. Modify rules for material safety to ensure that what escapes from products is safe under different use conditions and expand screening of toxicity to include chronic disease outcomes like diabetes, infertility, and harm to the immune and nervous systems. Determine if chemicals or materials like glass or stainless steel classified as inert leach into food. If they don’t leach, they’re not a priority for in-depth chemical analysis. Inert materials that can be reused should be the policy goal. The chemicals in Tier 1 provide the most reliable evidence that materials that come in contact with food are a source of people’s exposure to these chemicals, Muncke said. The chemicals are in people, they’re in food, and they’re in food-contact materials, she said. “What more proof do you want?” Inside Climate News asked the American Chemistry Council and Food Packaging Coalition, trade groups that represent the chemical and food-packing industries, if their members would release hazard information about the chemicals they use and phase out those known to be hazardous. Neither responded, but the Food Packaging Coalition maintains that packaging is designed to prevent the transfer of its components to food and to ensure that they are safe and suitable for their intended use. The paper offers a practical and transparent roadmap for using the best available evidence to prioritize food-contact chemicals for regulation, said Sara Lupolt, an expert on exposure assessment at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who was not involved in the research. Though not addressed in the paper, she added, more research is needed to determine which foods and chemical combinations result in more chemicals moving into food. Many of the chemicals that migrate into food are so-called non-intentionally added substances, (NIAS). Their identity is often obscure because existing tools can’t identify every chemical in use, especially when researchers don’t know what to look for because producers keep proprietary chemical ingredients secret. Muncke is particularly concerned about babies’ exposure to plastic chemicals in pouches that hold juices and pureed food. Earlier this year, her team found evidence that more than 330 chemicals leach from pouches, including nearly 80 known to be hazardous. They presented the findings at an event at the House of Lords in the United Kingdom in June. A greater volume of chemicals gets into baby food because the ratio of packaging to food is much greater in a small serving size, Muncke said. And the pouches are sterilized using heat, which drives chemicals to migrate and forms microplastics. Several peer-reviewed studies, including a 2023 Chemosphere study , also found chemicals, including NIAS, in baby food packaged in pouches. The paper’s authors believed the NIAS, which lacked adequate information to assess risk, were impurities and raw materials from producing plastic. “Infants may be constantly exposed to NIAS via consuming pouched food products,” the authors warned. For the 87 percent of chemicals that lack hazard data, it’s primarily a question of the data not being public, said study co-author Helene Wiesinger, a chemist and Food Packaging Forum scientific officer. That delays regulatory action, Wiesinger said, because governments and independent scientists must first figure out which chemicals are safe. She believes a product or chemical should not be allowed on the market until a company can prove that it’s safe. At a minimum, chemicals that have structural similarities with others known to be hazardous should be priorities for regulation, the paper argues. Seventy percent of the more than 4,200 chemicals the team classified into 38 priority groups — including PFAS, phthalates and organophosphates (used as flame retardants and pesticides, among other applications) — lack enough data to assess potential harms. Just because something isn’t yet known to be hazardous doesn’t mean it’s not hazardous, Wiesinger said. Time and again, chemicals found to present unreasonable risks are replaced with others that have similar properties and ultimately similar risks. “We hope this work provides practical guidance on how to at least not make the very obvious mistakes,” she said. readings.cn:
你的食物可能是安全的，但它的包装就是另一回事了。一项广泛的新研究揭示了为什么你应该尽可能避免使用塑料食品包装。

##段落

特别是婴儿食品袋，携带更高的化学暴露风险。杰弗里·格林伯格，环球图像集团通过盖蒂图片社

##段落

本文最初由《内部气候新闻》发布，作为气候台合作的一部分在此转载。大多数人通过检查冰箱里一桶老酸奶或橱柜后面罐头金枪鱼的保质期来决定它们是否还能安全食用。但没有任何标签表明农药、邻苯二甲酸盐、全氟和多氟烷基物质或其他危险化学物质可能从这些容器渗入你的食物。一项新的同行评审研究发现，在超过15000种与食物接触的化学物质中，有1222种对健康构成严重风险，如癌症和生殖损害。而绝大多数——87%，即超过13200种——缺乏足够的可获取信息来甚至评估其风险。

##段落

事实上，没有足够的公开信息让独立科学家评估可能污染食物的化学物质的安全性，这是“房间里的大象”，该研究的合著者、非营利组织食品包装论坛基金会董事总经理简·蒙克表示。该基金会领导了这项研究，该研究于周二发表在《环境科学与技术》杂志上。蒙克说，消费者相信，当监管机构允许化学物质用于食品包装等产品时，是因为它们经过了安全测试。“但事实并非如此，”她说，“而且这说不通。”

##段落

未参与该研究但与蒙克过去有过合作的独立化学安全与监管专家马里塞尔·马菲尼表示，该团队做了一项“非常非常好的工作”，强调了人们对影响每个人的物质风险知之甚少。马菲尼说，由于这项研究聚焦于行业和监管机构认为可靠的清单，它是在众所周知的灯柱下寻找。她说，虽然有大量信息表明这些化学物质中的许多不应上市或应受到更严格的监管，但该清单之外还有大量信息缺失。

##段落

在先前的工作中，蒙克和她的团队从美国、中国、日本以及欧洲和南美洲国家的监管机构批准的清单或研究中已识别的物质中，确定了超过15000种用于食品加工或包装的化学物质。蒙克说，在新论文中，他们分析了这个“令人瞠目结舌”的化学物质数量，以标记出最成问题的物质。为了最大化其优先级清单的实用性，该团队仅使用了从政府和监管机构获得的数据，将化学物质与

某些化学物质对人体健康构成危害，如致癌、损害生殖能力或在体内积聚。由此得出一份包含1，222种化学物质的优先清单，并按人类从食品接触材料中接触到的证据强度从高到低分为四个等级。其中，已知会渗入食品并在母乳、血液或其他人体样本中检测到的94种化学物质被列为第一等级，这是监管机构和公司考虑逐步淘汰的最高优先级。这些化学物质包括损害肝脏和免疫系统的全氟烷基物质（PFAS）“永久性化学物质”，它们使食品包装纸具有防油或防水性；可能致癌的苯乙烯，用于生产外卖包装和冷藏乳制品容器；干扰内分泌的邻苯二甲酸盐，用于增加塑料（如装植物油的那些塑料）的柔韧性；以及双酚A，添加于硬塑料和罐头内衬中，是内分泌干扰物在低剂量下就能损害发育的典型代表。研究发现，这些及其他化学物质会从容器渗入多种食品和饮料中，包括水、婴儿配方奶粉、橙汁、冰淇淋、酸奶和奶油、油类、蛋糕及高脂肪食品。下一高优先级清单（第二等级）还包括另外264种会渗入食品但尚未在生物监测研究中检测到的有害化学物质——至少目前还未检测到。食品包装论坛的专家表示，监管机构可以采取简单措施减少人们接触食品接触材料中发现或使用的有害化学物质，首先从不再逐一对单一化学物质进行评估开始。人们通过食品接触材料、纺织品、个人护理产品、空气污染等多种途径同时接触到多种合成化学物质。监管机构应引入“混合物分配系数”，建立安全边际，以考虑一次接触中多种化学物质的联合效应。化学物质应按类别进行监管。如果某一结构性质相似的化学物质组中个别成员有充分证据表明具有危害性，则该组所有成员都应撤出市场或未经证明安全前不予批准，正如欧盟在2023年提议将全氟烷基物质作为一个整体加以限制那样。修改材料安全规则，确保在不同使用条件下从产品中释放的物质是安全的，并将毒性筛查扩大到包括糖尿病、不孕症以及对免疫和神经系统的损害等慢性疾病结果。确定被归类为惰性的化学物质或材料（如玻璃或不锈钢）是否会渗入食品。如果没有渗漏，就不是进行深入化学分析的重点。可重复使用的惰性材料应成为政策目标。第一等级中的化学物质提供了……

蒙克表示，有最可靠的证据表明，接触食品的材料是人们接触这些化学物质的一个来源。她说，这些化学物质存在于人体内、食品中以及食品接触材料中。“你们还想要什么证据？”Inside Climate News询问了代表化学和食品包装行业的美国化学理事会和食品包装联盟，问其成员是否会公布他们使用的化学品的危害信息，并逐步淘汰已知有害的化学品。两者均未回应，但食品包装联盟坚持认为，包装的设计是为了防止其成分转移到食品中，并确保其安全且适合预期用途。约翰斯·霍普金斯大学布隆伯格公共卫生学院的暴露评估专家萨拉·卢波尔特表示，这篇论文提供了一条实用且透明的路线图，利用现有最佳证据优先对食品接触化学品进行监管，但她未参与这项研究。她补充说，尽管论文未涉及，但仍需更多研究来确定哪些食品和化学组合会导致更多化学物质迁移到食品中。许多迁移到食品中的化学物质是所谓的非有意添加物质（NIAS）。它们的身份往往不明确，因为现有工具无法识别使用中的每种化学物质，尤其是当研究人员不知道该寻找什么时，因为生产商对专有化学成分保密。蒙克特别关注婴儿通过装有果汁和果泥的包装袋接触塑料化学品的情况。今年早些时候，她的团队发现证据表明，超过330种化学物质从包装袋中浸出，其中包括近80种已知有害物质。他们在6月于英国上议院的一次活动中展示了这些发现。蒙克说，由于小份包装中包装与食品的比例更大，因此进入婴儿食品的化学物质数量更多。而且包装袋通过加热灭菌，这会促使化学物质迁移并形成微塑料。包括2023年《Chemosphere》研究在内的几项同行评审研究也发现，装在包装袋中的婴儿食品含有包括NIAS在内的化学物质。论文作者认为，缺乏足够信息评估风险的NIAS是塑料生产中的杂质和原材料。“婴儿可能通过食用袋装食品持续暴露于NIAS，”作者警告道。对于87%缺乏危害数据的化学物质，研究合著者、化学家兼食品包装论坛科学官员海伦·维辛格表示，这主要是数据不公开的问题。维辛格说，这延迟了监管行动，因为政府和独立科学家必须

第一步是要弄清楚哪些化学物质是安全的。她认为，在产品或化学物质被允许进入市场之前，公司必须能够证明其安全性。论文指出，至少，那些与已知有害物质具有结构相似性的化学物质应优先受到监管。该团队将超过4200种化学物质分类为38个优先组别，其中包括PFAS、邻苯二甲酸盐和有机磷酸酯（用作阻燃剂和农药等），其中70%缺乏足够的数据来评估潜在危害。维辛格表示，仅仅因为某物质尚未被认定为有害，并不意味着它无害。一次又一次，被发现有不可接受风险的化学物质被替换为具有类似性质、最终带来类似风险的替代品。她说：“我们希望这项工作能提供实用指导，至少避免犯下非常明显的错误。”##段落查看更多：气候健康公共卫生科学用最新的Vox填字游戏放松一下数据中心正在将美国人团结在一起播客一位福音派人士解释了人们对她的信仰的误解一个家伙制作了一个深度伪造应用，将女性照片变成裸体。结果并不顺利。我的学生认为用AI作弊没问题。也许他们说得有道理。邮箱（必填）注册提交您的邮箱即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: How to future-proof your wrists
body: 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google David Cox Modern life is ruining our wrists. We can all do something about it, but it helps to start early. It began with a dull ache. Over the course of a summer, it rapidly progressed to an arm-juddering pain, radiating through my left hand every time I struck a tennis ball or even attempted to open a door. I was 18 at that point, and playing competitive tennis was an important part of my life, but I'd just experienced an injury that would plague me for years. Now, nearly two decades later, it could increase my risk of developing wrist arthritis. Such problems are surprisingly common in mid to later life.  Our wrists are remarkably adaptable. They have the strength to allow us to lift heavy objects (including the World Record of  2,422 kg (5339 lbs) ), the flexibility to enable us to hit rogue balls during racquet sports, and the fine control to make tasks like painting possible. From typing to holding a coffee cup, functional wrists are essential to normal everyday life. But they are easily damaged, and we all need to start thinking about them earlier in life than you’d expect. Here's how to protect yours, so you can continue taking them for granted for years to come. We may think of the wrist as a single joint, but it is actually a complex , comprising multiple smaller joints. These are formed of eight small bones known as the carpal bones, the two long bones of the forearm, and the bases of the five metacarpal bones within the palm.  "Every ligament and every bone in the wrist that connects it to your forearm bones are really in a very finely-tuned balance," says Andrew Abadeer, an assistant professor at the University of South Florida. "When that goes awry, that's when wrist arthritis starts to develop." Injuries , combined with the effects of ageing , can disrupt this fragile equilibrium. Simply avoiding arthritis is a major reason for maintaining your wrist health. There are many different kinds, but it typically takes one of three forms: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis. The latter two ailments occur when the cartilage cushioning the small bones within the wrist becomes damaged, or the bones become misaligned. Both are linked to the long-term effects of injuries to the ligaments and bones within the wrist, or lingering inflammation due to overuse through repetitive manual tasks.  Sara Larsson, a researcher who studies wrist rehabilitation at Lund University, explains that this trauma may be as simple as a repetitive twisting movement or tripping and falling on an outstretched hand. "I see many people who had an injury when they were young, everything appeared to be fine again, and then 20 years later, they develop problems." Arthritis of the wrist has been estimated to affect as many as one in seven Americans . It is not only highly painful, but makes it harder for people to dress themselves and cut their own food, with the psychological burden being linked to depression. Abadeer describes the wrist as being a "sentinel joint" which can reflect early signs of declining health within the rest of the body. About half of all patients who develop rheumatoid arthritis first feel the effects the disease in their wrist before it progresses to other joints. Because the brain devotes a large region of the cortex, known as the cortical homunculus, to mapping the hands, wrist and fingers, grip strength can reflect brain structure and cognitive health. But people who reach their sixties with their wrists in better shape – typically assessed in the form of grip strength – tend to have better health overall. Those people are not only less frail and less vulnerable to falls, bone fractures and osteoporosis – a condition that weakens bones. But they are less likely to lose their independence in older age.   Before we get started, Jaehon Kim, an orthopaedic surgeon at the Ichan School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, recommends considering your diet. Foods high in calcium and other minerals, such as small, bony fish (sardines work well for this) and dairy products can help to mitigate against the development of osteoporosis. In addition, while weight might not seem particularly related to wrist health, shedding excess body fat can improve the overall biomechanics of the wrist joint. But overall, Larsson says that the best preventative measure is to do a few simple home-based workouts which can help make your wrist more resilient and stave off problems further down the line. For each of the below exercises, she recommends performing three sets of 10 repetitions (this means performing the exercise 10 times, resting, performing it again 10 times, resting, and doing it another 10 times), three or four times per week.  If you have any pre-existing conditions or injuries, it's important to seek medical advice before starting a new exercise regime. And if you feel pain at any point, stop and seek medical help.  The main muscles in your shoulders are known as the deltoids. While they may appear unrelated to wrists, Larsson says that strengthening the muscle groups across the whole arm can greatly benefit your wrist as they work together like a chain. "You don't just use your hand, you use the whole arm," says Larsson. "And if you're weak in your shoulders, then you put more load on the wrist. But if you are strong, then you can protect and unload the wrist." One easy method of training your shoulder muscles is simply to stand with your arms out to the sides, with your arms either straight or slightly bent. Slowly raise your arms up to the ceiling and then bring them down again slowly. Repeat this ten times. Grip strengthening exercises can improve wrist stability by conditioning groups of forearm muscles known as flexors and extensors, which attach to your fingers across the wrist joint, allowing you to grip objects. Studies have previously shown that this can also help people with existing wrist pain.  "All your forearm muscles connect into your hand on both sides of your wrist in a pulley system," says Abadeer. To work these muscles, you ideally want a hand therapy ball or therapeutic putty – a silicone-based material which you can squeeze in your hand – but a tennis ball will do. Hold the ball or putty in the palm of your hand and squeeze it as hard as you can for five to 10 seconds. Release the grip and relax your hand for another five seconds and then squeeze again. Repeat ten times in each hand. (Read more from the BBC about how grip strength can predict your chances of living to 100 .) According to Kim, another key means of reducing the stress on the wrist joints and tendons is exercises that flex and extend the wrist, using some form of mild weight or resistance as a load. This can also strengthen bones in the wrist, which could have longer-term health benefits, particularly when it comes to preventing a type of osteoporosis known as disuse osteopenia. "When they're loaded, these bones strengthen and start to remodel, adding more strength to the wall of that bone," says Abadeer. To do this, start by sitting and resting your forearm on a table with your hand hanging off the edge and holding a small weight, between 3 and 7kg (5 and 15lb). For a flexion exercise, have your palm facing upwards and curl your wrist up toward your body before lowering it back down again. For an extension exercise, have your palm facing downwards while holding the weight, and lift your hand up towards the ceiling before lowering it down again.  If you don't have weights, Larsson suggests using a resistance band instead. Fix one end of the band under a table leg and hold the other end across your wrist so you're experiencing some resistance while carrying out the exercises. Repeat both flexion and extension ten times. "I think this can go a long way in terms of helping the joints in your wrist, especially if you're typing and writing a lot," says Kim.   Lastly, there are supination and pronation movements. These can improve the range of motion of your wrist and its overall functionality. Like the flexion and extension exercises, they can be carried out over a table with a small weight or resistance band. Begin with your hand over the edge of the table with your thumb pointing up. Then slowly turn your wrist so your palm faces down, then return to the starting position, and rotate the other way so your palm faces up. Repeat this ten times. More like this: •  How to future-proof your hearing •  How to future-proof your brain for the 21st Century •  How to future-proof your knees   Abadeer says that such exercises are becoming increasingly important as we now live in what he describes as "a pronated world", where our hands spend many hours of the day in a fixed position, either due to typing on a laptop or a phone.  As with all our joints, strong, flexible wrists are something that we often take for granted. But as I found myself when my wrist was out of action for many months, it's only when you lose something that you realise its true importance. *  All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals. **A previous version of this article included an incorrect figure for the heaviest weight ever lifted. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Health Human body Science Features

16小时前 分享 保存 在Google上设为偏好 David Cox 现代生活正在毁掉我们的手腕。我们都能为此做点什么，但尽早开始会更有帮助。一切始于隐隐作痛。在一个夏天的时间里，它迅速恶化为一种令手臂颤抖的剧痛，每当我击打网球或甚至试图开门时，疼痛便从左手中辐射而出。那时我18岁，打竞技网球是我生活中的重要部分，但我刚刚经历了一次将困扰我多年的伤病。如今，近二十年过去，它可能增加我患上手腕关节炎的风险。这类问题在中年及以后的生活中出奇地普遍。

##段落 我们的手腕具有惊人的适应能力。它们拥有让我们举起重物（包括2,422公斤（5339磅）的世界纪录）的力量，具备在球拍运动中击打刁钻球的灵活性，以及使绘画等任务成为可能的精细控制力。从打字到握咖啡杯，功能健全的手腕对日常生活的正常运转至关重要。但它们很容易受损，而且我们都需要在比预期更早的人生阶段开始关注它们。以下是如何保护你的手腕，以便你能在未来的岁月里继续视其为理所当然。

##段落 我们可能将手腕视为一个单一关节，但它实际上是一个复杂的结构，由多个较小的关节组成。这些关节由八块被称为腕骨的小骨、前臂的两根长骨以及手掌内五块掌骨的基底部构成。“手腕中每一根韧带和每一块连接前臂骨骼的骨头，都处于一种非常精妙的平衡状态，”南佛罗里达大学助理教授Andrew Abadeer说。“当这种平衡被打破时，手腕关节炎就开始发展了。”损伤加上衰老的影响，会破坏这种脆弱的平衡。

##段落 仅仅避免关节炎就是维持手腕健康的一个主要原因。关节炎有许多不同类型，但通常表现为三种形式之一：类风湿性关节炎、骨关节炎或创伤后关节炎。后两种疾病发生在手腕内小骨之间的软骨缓冲受损或骨骼错位时。两者都与手腕内韧带和骨骼损伤的长期影响有关，或因重复性体力劳动过度使用而导致的持续炎症有关。隆德大学研究手腕康复的研究员Sara Larsson解释说，这种创伤可能简单到如重复扭转动作或绊倒时用手撑地。“我看到许多人在年轻时受过伤，一切似乎又恢复正常，但二十年后，他们开始出现问题。”手腕关节炎已被证实与这些因素密切相关。

据估计，多达七分之一的美国人受到影响。这不仅极其痛苦，还使人们更难自己穿衣和切食物，其心理负担与抑郁症有关。阿巴迪尔将手腕描述为一个“哨兵关节”，可以反映身体其他部位健康状况恶化的早期迹象。大约一半的类风湿性关节炎患者首先在手腕上感受到疾病的影响，然后才发展到其他关节。由于大脑将一大片皮层区域（称为皮层侏儒）用于映射手、手腕和手指，握力可以反映大脑结构和认知健康。但那些年过六十、手腕状况更好——通常以握力形式评估——的人，往往整体健康状况更佳。他们不仅不那么脆弱，也不那么容易跌倒、骨折和患上骨质疏松症——一种削弱骨骼的疾病。而且他们在老年时期失去独立性的可能性也更小。在我们开始之前，纽约西奈山伊坎医学院的骨科外科医生杰洪·金建议考虑你的饮食。富含钙和其他矿物质的食物，如小鱼带骨鱼（沙丁鱼对此很有效）和乳制品，有助于缓解骨质疏松症的发展。此外，虽然体重看起来与手腕健康关系不大，但减掉多余体脂可以改善手腕关节的整体生物力学。但总体而言，拉尔森表示，最好的预防措施是做一些简单的居家锻炼，这可以帮助你的手腕更具韧性，并避免日后出现更多问题。对于以下每项练习，她建议每次进行三组，每组10次重复（这意味着执行练习10次，休息，再执行10次，休息，再做10次），每周三到四次。如果你已有任何现有疾病或损伤，在开始新的锻炼计划前务必寻求医疗建议。如果在任何时候感到疼痛，请停止并寻求医疗帮助。你肩膀的主要肌肉被称为三角肌。虽然它们看起来与手腕无关，但拉尔森表示，加强整个手臂的肌肉群可以大大有益于你的手腕，因为它们像链条一样协同工作。“你不仅仅使用手，你使用整个手臂，”拉尔森说。“如果你的肩膀力量弱，那么手腕就会承受更多负荷。但如果你强壮，那么你可以保护并减轻手腕的负担。”一种锻炼肩部肌肉的简单方法是站立，双臂向两侧伸展，手臂可以伸直或略微弯曲。慢慢抬起你的……

双臂向上举至天花板，然后缓慢放下。重复十次。握力强化练习可以通过锻炼前臂肌群（即屈肌和伸肌）来改善手腕稳定性，这些肌肉通过腕关节附着在手指上，使你能够抓握物体。先前的研究表明，这也有助于缓解已有的手腕疼痛。“你所有的前臂肌肉通过腕关节两侧的滑轮系统连接到手部，”阿巴迪尔说。要锻炼这些肌肉，理想情况下你需要一个手部治疗球或治疗性腻子——一种可以握在手中挤压的硅基材料——但网球也可以。将球或腻子放在手掌中，尽可能用力挤压五到十秒。松开握力，放松手部五秒，然后再次挤压。每只手重复十次。（从BBC了解更多关于握力如何预测你活到100岁的几率。）据金姆介绍，减轻腕关节和肌腱压力的另一个关键方法是进行手腕屈伸练习，使用某种轻度重量或阻力作为负荷。这还可以增强手腕骨骼，可能带来长期的健康益处，尤其是在预防一种被称为废用性骨量减少的骨质疏松症方面。“当这些骨骼受到负荷时，它们会增强并开始重塑，增加骨骼壁的强度，”阿巴迪尔说。要进行这项练习，先坐下，将前臂放在桌子上，手悬在边缘外，握住一个小重量，约3至7公斤（5至15磅）。对于屈曲练习，手掌朝上，将手腕向上卷向身体，然后放下。对于伸展练习，手掌朝下握住重量，将手向上举向天花板，然后放下。如果没有重量，拉尔森建议使用阻力带代替。将带子的一端固定在桌腿下，另一端横跨手腕握住，这样在练习时会感受到一些阻力。重复屈曲和伸展各十次。“我认为这对帮助手腕关节大有裨益，尤其是如果你经常打字和写字，”金姆说。最后是旋后和旋前动作。这些动作可以改善手腕的活动范围和整体功能。与屈伸练习类似，可以在桌子上用小重量或阻力带进行。开始时，手悬在桌子边缘外，拇指朝上。然后慢慢转动手腕，使手掌朝下，返回起始位置，然后向另一方向旋转。

将手掌朝上。重复这个动作十次。更多类似内容：• 如何为你的听力做好未来防护 • 如何为你的大脑做好21世纪的未来防护 • 如何为你的膝盖做好未来防护  
阿巴迪尔表示，这类锻炼正变得越来越重要，因为我们如今生活在一个他称之为“旋前世界”的环境中，双手每天有许多小时都处于固定姿势，无论是打字使用笔记本电脑还是手机。  
与所有关节一样，强壮且灵活的手腕常常被我们视为理所当然。但正如我亲身经历的那样，当我的手腕数月无法活动时，我才意识到，只有失去某样东西时，你才会真正体会到它的重要性。  
* 本文所有内容仅供一般信息参考，不应被视为替代医疗保健专业人士建议的用途。  
**本文的先前版本曾包含一个关于举重最重纪录的错误数字。  
——如需获取值得信赖的健康与福祉见解，请订阅资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》新闻通讯，她还开设了《活得更久更好》与《平静六步法》课程。

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. Plus: Click here for a chance to get your own work question answered on the show! Listen to Fixable now wherever you get your podcasts.
About the author Hayley Caldwell is a copywriter on the Audience Development team at TED.

##段落
感觉被老板忽视？你可以这样做  
2023年6月15日  
/  
海莉·考德威尔  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
Stocksy  

##段落
你是否曾经有过这样的经历：你的努力工作——包括你的成功——被经理视而不见？TED的新播客《Fixable》正是为此而生——帮助那些带着职场烦恼来电的普通人解决问题。

##段落
在第四集中，联合主持人兼顶级领导力教练弗朗西丝·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯认识了来电者奈阿。在一次重大重组后，她与一位忙碌的新老板搭档，一直难以获得认可。奈阿尽心尽力地把工作做好，但缺乏对她工作的认可、鼓励——甚至关注——让她逐渐失去动力。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看清事情的人性面——也看清你经理的人性面。

##段落
“有时候，阻碍你与经理成为优秀合作伙伴的，可能是对现状仍存有的一些残余挫败感，”安妮解释道。“但那种情绪对你不会有帮助。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿认识到经理的人性，并原谅他们犯错。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮还分享了这样一个策略供她练习：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西丝是这样说的：“你在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。所以如果你对经理有评判，你就无法真正对他们的处境感到好奇。而当你把经理看作一个身兼多份兼职的人时，我们该如何帮助他们走向成功？”

##段落
“好奇心——在工作场所中真正神奇的灵丹妙药——最简单的表达形式就是提问，”安妮说。例如，你可以先问问经理，用什么方式让他们了解你的成就和贡献最有效。或者，你也可以专注于如何让你们的会面更高效，问问他们：“我们的一对一交流如何能为我们共同要实现的目标服务？”

##段落
另一个选择：坦诚表达你的担忧，并询问经理他们对你成功的愿景是什么样子的。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是：我非常努力地工作，在这种变动不定的状态下，我担心六个月过去了，人们会怀疑我是否把工作做好了。所以对我来说，明确‘什么才算做好工作，以及我如何帮你获得这些信息？’会很有帮助。”

##段落
跨行业、跨地域，许多人都正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力，需要经历一段重新调整期，这都是正常的。

从提问开始——把老板视为与你合作的普通人——可以帮助你重新获得一些主动权与自主性。  
“试着做你能做的，然后惊叹于对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一张你希望对方如何改变的清单，”弗朗西斯说。“我认为你会惊喜地发现；这正是这件事的美好之处。”  
无论你从事何种工作或经营何种业务，你都能在《Fixable》中找到可操作的建议，改善你的工作日。在其他集数中，学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩展你的副业项目，以及主持更有成效的会议。另外：点击此处，有机会在节目中让你的工作问题得到解答！现在就在你获取播客的任何平台收听《Fixable》。

readings.title: Is New York's cannabis business flying high?
body: 26 March 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mike Wendling Five years after it was legalised in the state, cannabis is seemingly everywhere in New York. But, business owners say that many legitimate outlets are struggling – largely because of a thriving grey market, and the complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry. If you've recently visited New York, you've probably noticed something.  Advertisements outside bodegas display pictures of bright green flowers, higher-end dispensaries that resemble coffee bars or electronics shops welcome customers from all over the world, and then of course there's the smell – so seemingly omnipresent that even US Open tennis players have complained .  Weed is everywhere. From the outside it looks like a free-for-all, one that is drawing scepticism even from voices broadly supportive of the aims of the legalisation – including reducing harm and boosting tax revenue. Social media is rife with complaints (typical comments include "New York could not have screwed up legal weed any worse!") and for years the local press has been chronicling the rise of the "weed bodega" – typically a corner store selling products of dubious provenance. Across the country, weed consumption has increased – though studies indicate  that the rate of young people using has gradually declined since the turn of the century.  Things may have come to a head recently when the  New York Times , once a legal weed supporter, published an editorial headlined: "Marijuana Is Everywhere. That's a Problem." The newspaper now argues that "marijuana is causing more harm than predicted" and calls for tighter regulation.  But this new green rush is not as straightforward as it seems. Business owners say that public perceptions have been sullied by illegal operators, and that many above-board businesses are struggling – largely because of the incredibly complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry.  "At first glance, New York's cannabis industry appears to be booming," says Jayson Tantalo, a cannabis businessman and vice president of operations for the New York Cannabis Retail Association. "But that perception was initially driven by an oversaturation of illicit operators.  "These shops often presented themselves as legitimate, creating a misleading sense of scale and economic success," he says.  New York state legalised recreational use of cannabis five years ago this month . But legal wrangling and slow issuing of licenses hampered initial growth, while sales in other states such as California were racing ahead.   The bottleneck was so restrictive that some growers in New York complained that their crops were going to waste because of the lack of retail sales outlets. Meanwhile hundreds of those shady outlets sprang up, particularly in New York City.  Those wild days may be coming to an end. State authorities are starting to crack down on illegal operators, and police have been given power to immediately shut shops without a licence. And more legal businesses are being set up to address pent-up demand.  "It was really out of control," says Vlad Bautista, co-founder of Happy Munkey, a cannabis retailer in the Inwood neighbourhood of Manhattan.  "It made a little dent," he says of recent enforcement efforts. "But there’s still a long way to go." CRB Monitor, a firm that researches the cannabis industry, counts more than 2,000 active cannabis business licenses across the state – including retailers, wholesalers, growers and other types of cannabis companies – with another nearly 5,000 applications in the pipeline.  The effects can be seen far from Manhattan with weed shops popping up all across a state that is roughly the size of England.  Jayson Tantalo owns one of them. He was involved in the weed business long before it was legal. "What started as survival evolved into deep expertise in the industry," he says. He and his wife Britni set up their Flower City Dispensary retail business in Victor, a suburban community in western New York state with a population of about 16,000.  Tantalo says that while the industry is "highly visible and normalised" across the state, only a small percentage of legal operators have captured large shares of the market.  "Growth exists, but it's constrained, uneven, and still stabilising," he says.  New York's growing pains are just one example of the extraordinarily complicated legal status of cannabis that has caused confusion across the country - for businesses, customers and the public.  The patchwork legal regime around the industry is a product of cannabis's long strange trip from respectability to contraband and back again. George Washington, the first US president, famously grew hemp crops at his estate.   But waves of restrictions followed, culminating in a 1970 law that deemed marijuana a Schedule I drug – the most restrictive category.  Despite the US government's war on drugs, there has always been a significant movement calling for looser regulations on cannabis. That movement gradually became more mainstream in the early years of this century.  Support for legalising cannabis first cracked 50% of Americans in 2013, according to polling firm Gallup, and that figure has since risen to more than two-thirds today.  But instead of blanket legalisation, reforms came in piecemeal fashion, on the state and sometimes even the local level, creating a fragmented state-by-state market.  To top it off, weed remains illegal under federal law – thousands of people still get arrested each year for marijuana possession and related crimes.  This legal patchwork results in some bizarre consequences. A road-tripper heading west from New York would pass through Pennsylvania, where recreational use of marijuana is illegal, and then into Ohio, where it was legalised by a 2023 referendum. If they continued along Interstate 80 they would eventually get to Indiana (where weed is illegal), Illinois (legal), and Iowa (illegal) – and so on.  That's confusing in itself. But another legal loophole has opened the door for all sorts of grey-market and online businesses, effectively making cannabis accessible to nearly everyone in the country.  The 2018 Farm Bill legalised hemp with a relatively low level of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC – the chemical that gets cannabis users high.  Hemp contains CBD – a chemical that doesn’t produce the high of THC but has some health benefits. A glut of CBD ensued. And in a lab, CBD can be converted into psychoactive THC.  "Entrepreneurs could say, 'this is just hemp', even if what they were producing was a highly intoxicating form of THC," says Chris Lindsay, vice president of policy and state advocacy for the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp (ATACH), which represents licenced businesses.  Those products are sold online or in those weed bodegas – even in states that have not legalised marijuana.  Robin Goldstein, an economist at the University of California-Davis and co-author of the book Can Legal Weed Win?: The Blunt Realities of Cannabis Economics, estimates that just behind California, the second-biggest weed market is in Texas, despite the Lone Star state's blanket ban on recreational cannabis use.  Business owners like Jason Ambrosino, have become used to dealing with spiralling legal complexities.  Ambrosino is founder and chief executive of Veterans Holdings, a weed business based in Gloversville, New York, about three hours north of New York City. An army vet who was seriously injured in Iraq, he got into the cannabis industry after discovering that medical marijuana was effective in alleviating his pain. These days, he says his legal headaches include rules that make it impossible to branch out into neighbouring states or to obtain traditional sources of financing.  "There’s a million different ways to get institutional funding, but you can’t get any of those for cannabis because of federal law," he says.  Despite the headwinds, Ambrosino has managed to grow his business and now employs around 80 people, and is hopeful that the increased licences for legal shops in New York will mean more sales opportunities down the line.  Vlad Bautista, the Happy Munkey co-founder, roughly estimates that he spends 40% of his time complying with various regulations, and, in particular, he questions some of the rules around advertising and tax law.  "If you own a cannabis business, you have much stricter advertising regulations than companies selling alcohol, cigarettes or gambling," he says. "You're stuck in the stone age, handing out flyers on the street." A buzz ran through the industry in December of last year, when President Trump signed an executive order which directed officials to accelerate efforts to reclassify marijuana to a less stringent category.  That might eventually give cannabis businesses some added profits – due to another federal law, weed companies aren't able to deduct all of their normal business expenses from their taxes. But businesspeople and experts aren't holding their breath for a practical impact any time soon.  "It's smoke and mirrors," says Naomi Granger, founder and chief executive of the National Association of Cannabis Accounting and Tax Professionals, who says some headlines heralding a new dawn for the cannabis industry have been somewhat misleading.  Some industry insiders say uncertainty is part and parcel of a nascent industry.  Steve Kemmerling, founder and chief executive of CRB Monitor, notes that states that were earlier to legal weed – California and Colorado in the western US were among the first – experienced hiccups on the way to relative stability.  "In any new market you're going to have wild volatility and price swings, mergers and acquisitions, along with competitive businesses and people cutting corners," he says.  And in a buzzy industry perhaps it's not surprising to encounter businesspeople who seem hard wired for sunny-day thinking.  "I'm an optimist," says Vlad Bautista. "We live in a divided and polarised world where nobody agrees on everything, and when you look at public opinion, there's a majority of people who agree on legal cannabis." "We've made a ton of progress," he says, "but there's still a long way to go." 在纽约州合法化五年后，大麻似乎无处不在。但企业主表示，许多合法门店正举步维艰——主要归因于蓬勃发展的灰色市场，以及美国大麻产业复杂的法律地位。

如果你最近去过纽约，你可能会注意到一些现象。杂货店外的广告展示着亮绿色花朵的图片，高端药房形似咖啡吧或电子产品店，欢迎着来自世界各地的顾客，当然还有那气味——似乎无处不在，连美国网球公开赛的选手都抱怨过。大麻无处不在。

从表面看，这像是一场无序竞争，甚至引来了一些原本支持合法化目标（包括减少危害和增加税收）的声音的质疑。社交媒体上充斥着抱怨（典型评论如“纽约不可能把合法大麻搞得更糟了！”），多年来当地媒体一直在报道“大麻杂货店”的兴起——这类店铺通常销售来源可疑的产品。全美范围内，大麻消费量有所增加——尽管研究表明，自世纪之交以来，年轻人的使用率已逐渐下降。

事情最近可能达到了顶点，《纽约时报》——曾是合法大麻的支持者——发表了一篇题为“大麻无处不在。这是个问题。”的社论。该报现在认为“大麻造成的危害比预期的更大”，并呼吁加强监管。

但这场新的绿色热潮并不像表面看起来那么简单。企业主表示，公众看法已被非法经营者玷污，许多合法企业正面临困境——主要归因于美国大麻产业极其复杂的法律地位。

“乍一看，纽约的大麻产业似乎在蓬勃发展，”大麻商人兼纽约大麻零售协会运营副总裁Jayson Tantalo说。“但这种看法最初是由非法经营者的过度饱和所推动的。”

“这些店铺往往伪装成合法经营，制造了一种关于规模和经济效益的误导性印象，”他说。

纽约州在本月迎来了娱乐用大麻合法化五周年。但法律纠纷和许可证发放缓慢阻碍了初期增长，而加利福尼亚等其他州的销售却在飞速发展。这一瓶颈如此严格，以至于一些纽约种植者抱怨，由于缺乏零售销售渠道，他们的作物正在浪费。与此同时，数百家那些可疑店铺如雨后春笋般涌现，尤其是在

在纽约市，那些狂野的日子可能即将结束。州当局开始打击非法经营者，警方已被授权立即关闭无照商店。同时，更多合法企业正在设立，以满足被压抑的需求。“当时真的失控了，”曼哈顿因伍德区大麻零售商Happy Munkey的联合创始人弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说。谈到近期的执法行动，他表示“这起了一点作用，但还有很长的路要走。”研究大麻行业的公司CRB Monitor统计，全州有超过2000个活跃的大麻商业许可证——包括零售商、批发商、种植者及其他类型的大麻公司——另有近5000份申请正在审批中。这种影响远远超出了曼哈顿，在这个面积大致相当于英格兰的州内，大麻商店遍地开花。杰森·坦塔洛就是其中一位店主。他在大麻合法化之前很久就涉足这一行业。“最初是为了生存，后来演变成对行业的深入了解，”他说。他和妻子布里特尼在纽约州西部维克多郊区社区（人口约16000）开设了他们的Flower City Dispensary零售店。坦塔洛表示，尽管该行业在全州“高度可见且已常态化”，但只有少数合法经营者占据了较大市场份额。“增长存在，但受到限制、不均衡，且仍在稳定过程中，”他说。纽约的成长阵痛只是大麻极其复杂法律地位的一个例子，这种状况已在全美范围内给企业、消费者和公众造成困惑。围绕该行业的零散法律体系，源于大麻从体面到违禁品再回归的漫长奇异旅程。美国第一任总统乔治·华盛顿以在其庄园种植大麻而闻名。但随后一波波限制接踵而至，最终在1970年的一项法律中，大麻被列为第一类管制药物——即最严格的类别。尽管美国政府发起禁毒战争，但一直有重要运动呼吁放宽对大麻的管制。本世纪初，这场运动逐渐走向主流。根据民调公司盖洛普的数据，2013年，支持大麻合法化的美国人比例首次突破50%，而如今这一数字已升至三分之二以上。但改革并非全面合法化，而是在州甚至地方层面零敲碎打地推进，形成了各州各自为政的碎片化市场。更糟的是，大麻在联邦法律下仍属非法——每年仍有数千人因持有大麻及相关犯罪被捕。这种法律拼凑局面……

法律工作的结果有时会引发一些奇怪的现象。一名从纽约向西出发的公路旅行者会穿过宾夕法尼亚州，在那里娱乐用大麻是非法的，然后进入俄亥俄州，那里在2023年的公投中将其合法化。如果他们继续沿80号州际公路行驶，最终会到达印第安纳州（大麻非法）、伊利诺伊州（合法）和爱荷华州（非法），如此反复。这本身就令人困惑。但另一个法律漏洞为各种灰色市场和在线业务打开了大门，实际上使美国几乎所有人都能接触到这种物质。

2018年的农业法案将四氢大麻酚（THC）含量相对较低的大麻合法化，THC是让大麻使用者产生兴奋感的化学物质。大麻含有CBD——一种不会产生THC那种兴奋感但具有某些健康益处的化学物质。随后CBD出现了过剩。而在实验室中，CBD可以转化为具有精神活性的THC。美国大麻和大麻贸易协会（ATACH）的政策和州宣传副总裁克里斯·林赛表示：“企业家们可以说‘这只是大麻’，即使他们生产的是高度致醉形式的THC。”ATACH代表持牌企业。这些产品在网上或在那些大麻杂货店出售，即使在未将大麻合法化的州也是如此。

加州大学戴维斯分校的经济学家、《合法大麻能赢吗？：大麻经济的直率现实》一书的合著者罗宾·戈德斯坦估计，仅次于加利福尼亚州，第二大大麻市场是德克萨斯州，尽管孤星州全面禁止娱乐用大麻。像杰森·安布罗西诺这样的企业主已经习惯于应对日益复杂的法律问题。安布罗西诺是总部位于纽约州格洛弗斯维尔的大麻企业Veterans Holdings的创始人兼首席执行官，该地距离纽约市以北约三小时车程。他是一名在伊拉克严重受伤的退伍军人，在发现医用大麻能有效缓解他的疼痛后进入了这一行业。如今，他说他的法律头疼问题包括一些规则，这些规则使他无法扩展到邻近州或获得传统的融资来源。

他说：“有无数种方式可以获得机构资金，但由于联邦法律，你无法为大麻获得任何一种。”尽管面临这些逆风，安布罗西诺还是成功发展了他的业务，现在雇佣了大约80名员工，并对纽约合法商店牌照的增加将意味着未来更多销售机会抱有希望。Happy Munkey联合创始人弗拉德·巴蒂斯塔粗略估计，他花费40%的时间来遵守各种法规，特别是质疑一些关于广告和税法的规则。“如果你拥有一家大麻……”

他指出：“相比销售酒类、香烟或赌博产品的公司，你的广告监管要严格得多。你就像困在石器时代，只能在街上发传单。”去年十二月，特朗普总统签署了一项行政命令，指示官员加速将大麻重新归类到更宽松的类别，这在整个行业引起了轰动。这最终可能为大麻企业带来额外利润——因为根据另一项联邦法律，大麻公司无法从税收中扣除所有正常业务开支。但商界人士和专家并未急于期待近期内产生实际影响。全国大麻会计与税务专业人士协会的创始人兼首席执行官娜奥米·格兰杰表示：“这不过是烟雾弹。”她认为，一些预示大麻行业新纪元的头条新闻有些误导性。一些业内人士表示，不确定性是新行业的固有特征。CRB Monitor的创始人兼首席执行官史蒂夫·凯默林指出，较早合法化大麻的州——美国西部的加利福尼亚和科罗拉多是首批之一——在走向相对稳定的过程中经历了波折。他说：“在任何新市场中，你都会遇到剧烈的波动和价格震荡、并购活动，以及竞争激烈的企业和偷工减料的行为。”在这个喧嚣的行业中，遇到似乎天生乐观的企业家或许并不奇怪。“我是个乐观主义者，”弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说。“我们生活在一个分裂和两极分化的世界里，没有人能在所有事情上达成一致，但当你观察公众舆论时，大多数人同意大麻合法化。”“我们已经取得了很大进展，”他说，“但前路依然漫长。”如需药物成瘾支持，请访问BBC Action Line。——如需全球洞察和专家分析，供董事会及其他领域使用，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《基本清单》则提供精选特写和见解。欲了解更多商业及更多内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业毒品特写

readings.title: My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something.
body: Advice My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something. ﻿To save the humanities, we need to rethink our assumptions about AI — and education. by Sigal Samuel Updated Sep 6, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Gift Pete Gamlen for Vox Part Of The rapid development of AI has benefits — and poses serious risks see all updates Sigal Samuel is a correspondent for Vox’s Future Perfect. She writes primarily about the future of consciousness, tracking advances in artificial intelligence and neuroscience and their staggering ethical implications. Before joining Vox, Sigal was the religion editor at the Atlantic. Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year. This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here . I am a university teaching assistant, leading discussion sections for large humanities lecture classes. This also means I grade a lot of student writing — and, inevitably, see a lot of AI writing too. Of course, many of us are working on developing assignments and pedagogies to make that less tempting. But as a TA, I only have limited ability to implement these policies. And in the meantime, AI-generated writing is so ubiquitous that to take course policy on it seriously, or even to escalate every suspected instance to the professor who runs the course, would be to make dozens of accusations, some of them false positives, for basically every assignment. I believe in the numinous, ineffable value of a humanities education, but I’m also not going to convince stressed 19-year-olds of that value by cracking down hard on something everyone does. How do I think about the ethics of enforcing the rules of an institution that they don’t take seriously, or letting things slide in the name of building a classroom that feels less like an obstacle to circumvent? Dear Troubled Teacher, I know you said you believe in the “ineffable value of a humanities education,” but if we want to actually get clear on your dilemma, that ineffable value must be effed! So: What is the real value of a humanities education? Looking at the modern university, one might think the humanities aren’t so different from the STEM fields. Just as the engineering department or the math department justifies its existence by pointing to the products it creates — bridge designs, weather forecasts — humanities departments nowadays justify their existence by noting that their students create products, too: literary interpretations, cultural criticism, short films. But let’s be real: It’s the neoliberalization of the university that has forced the humanities into that weird contortion. That’s never what they were supposed to be. Their real aim, as the philosopher Megan Fritts writes , is “the formation of human persons.” In other words, while the purpose of other departments is ultimately to create a product, a humanities education is meant to be different, because the student herself is the product. She is what’s getting created and recreated by the learning process. Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here! This vision of education — as a pursuit that’s supposed to be personally transformative — is what Aristotle proposed back in ancient Greece. He believed the real goal was not to impart knowledge, but to cultivate the virtues: honesty, justice, courage, and all the other character traits that make for a flourishing life. But because flourishing is devalued in our hypercapitalist society, you find yourself caught between that original vision and today’s product-based, utilitarian vision. And students sense — rightly! — that generative AI proves the utilitarian vision for the humanities is a sham. As one student said to his professor at New York University, in an effort to justify using AI to do his work for him , “You’re asking me to go from point A to point B, why wouldn’t I use a car to get there?” It’s a completely logical argument — as long as you accept the utilitarian vision. The real solution, then, is to be honest about what the humanities are for: You’re in the business of helping students with the cultivation of their character. I know, I know: Lots of students will say, “I don’t have time to work on cultivating my character! I just need to be able to get a job!” It’s totally fair for them to be focusing on their job prospects. But your job is to focus on something else — something that will help them flourish in the long run, even if they don’t fully see the value in it now. Your job is to be their Aristotle. For the ancient Greek philosopher, the mother of all virtues was phronesis , or practical wisdom. And I’d argue there’s nothing more useful you can do for your students than help them cultivate this virtue, which is made more, not less, relevant by the advent of AI. Practical wisdom goes beyond just knowing general rules — “don’t lie,” for example — and applying them mechanically like some sort of moral robot . It’s about knowing how to make good judgments when faced with the complex, dynamic situations life throws at you. Sometimes that’ll actually mean violating a classic rule (in certain cases, you should lie !). If you’ve honed your practical wisdom, you’ll be able to discern the morally salient features of a particular situation and come up with a response that’s well-attuned to that context. This is exactly the sort of deliberation that students will need to be good at as they step into the wider world. The breakneck pace of technological innovation means they’re going to have to choose, again and again and again, how to make use of emerging technologies — and how not to. The best training they can get now is training in how to wisely make this type of choice. Unfortunately, that’s exactly what using generative AI in the classroom threatens to short-circuit, because it removes something incredibly valuable: friction . Encountering friction is how we give our cognitive muscles a workout. Taking it out of the picture makes things easier in the short term, but in the long term, it can lead to intellectual deskilling, where our cognitive muscles gradually become weaker for lack of use. “Practical wisdom is built up by practice just like all the other virtues, so if you don’t have the opportunity to reason and don’t have practice in deliberating about certain things, you won’t be able to deliberate well later,” philosopher of technology Shannon Vallor told me last year. “We need a lot of cognitive exercise in order to develop practical wisdom and retain it. And there is reason to worry about cognitive automation depriving us of the opportunity to build and retain those cognitive muscles.” So, how do you help your students retain and build their phronesis? You add friction back in, by giving them as many opportunities as possible to practice deliberating and choosing. If I were designing the curriculum, I wouldn’t do that by adopting a strict “no AI” policy. Instead, I’d be honest with students about the real benefit of the humanities and about why mindless AI cheating would be cheating themselves out of that benefit. Then, I’d offer them two choices when it comes time to write an essay: They can either write it with help from AI, or without. Both are totally fine. But if they do get help from AI, they have to also write an in-class reflection piece, explaining why they chose to use a chatbot and how they think it changed their thinking and learning process. I’d make it shorter than the original assignment but longer than a paragraph, so it forces them to develop the very reasoning skills they were trying to avoid using. As a TA, you could suggest this to professors, but they may not go for it. Unfortunately, you’ve got limited agency here (unless you’re willing to risk your job or walk away from it). All you can do in such a situation is exercise the agency you do have. So use every bit of it. Since you lead discussion sections, you’re well-placed to prompt your students to work their cognitive muscles in conversation. You could even stage a debate about AI: Assign half of them to argue the case for using chatbots to write papers and half of them to argue the opposite. If a professor insists on a strict “no AI” policy, and you encounter essays that seem clearly AI-written, you may have little choice but to report them. But if there’s room for doubt about a given essay, you might err on the side of leniency if the student has engaged very thoughtfully in the discussion. At least then you know they’ve achieved the most important aim. None of this is easy. I feel for you and all other educators who are struggling in this confusing environment. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if some educators are suffering from moral injury , a psychological condition that arises when you feel you’ve been forced to violate your own values. But maybe it can comfort you to remember that this is much bigger than you. Generative AI is an existential threat to a humanities education as currently constituted. Over the next few years, humanities departments will have to paradigm-shift or perish. If they want to survive, they’ll need to get brutally honest about their true mission. For now, from your pre-paradigm-shift perch, all you can do is make the choices that are left for you to make. I went back to Shannon Vallor’s first book, Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting . If there’s one book I could get everyone in the AI world to read, it would be this one. And I think it can be useful to everyone else, too, because we all need to cultivate what Vallor calls the “technomoral virtues” — the traits that will allow us to adapt well to emerging technologies. A New Yorker piece about AI and cognitive atrophy led me to a 2024 psychology paper titled “The Unpleasantness of Thinking: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Association Between Mental Effort and Negative Affect.” The authors’ conclusion: “We suggest that mental effort is inherently aversive.” Come again? Yes, sometimes I just want to turn off my brain and watch Netflix, but sometimes thinking about a challenging topic is so pleasurable! To me, it feels like running or weightlifting: Too much is exhausting, but the right amount is exhilarating. And what feels like “the right amount” can go up or down depending on how much I practice. Astrobiologist Sara Imari Walker published an essay in Noema provocatively titled “ AI Is Life .” She reminds us that evolution produced us and we produced AI. “It is therefore part of the same ancient lineage of information that emerged with the origin of life,” she writes. “Technology is not artificially replacing life — it is life.” To be clear, she’s not arguing that tech is alive; she’s saying it’s an outgrowth of human life, an extension of our own species. This story was originally published in The Highlight , Vox’s member-exclusive magazine. To get early access to member-exclusive stories every month, join the Vox Membership program today . 我的学生们认为用AI作弊没问题。也许他们发现了什么。为了拯救人文学科，我们需要重新思考对AI——以及教育——的假设。作者：西格尔·塞缪尔 更新于2026年9月6日，UTC时间中午12:00 礼物 皮特·甘伦为Vox绘制 部分 AI的快速发展带来了好处——也带来了严重风险 查看所有更新 西格尔·塞缪尔是Vox“未来完美”栏目的记者。她主要撰写关于意识未来的文章，追踪人工智能和神经科学的进展及其令人震惊的伦理影响。加入Vox之前，西格尔是《大西洋月刊》的宗教编辑。编者按，9月6日东部时间上午8点：在西格尔·塞缪尔休产假期间，我们为您带来一些最受欢迎的“里程可能因人而异”专栏。以下这篇最初发表于去年。这期非传统建议专栏为您提供了一个独特的框架，用来思考道德困境。它基于价值多元主义：即我们每个人都拥有多种价值，这些价值同样有效，但常常相互冲突。在此提交您自己的问题。我是一名大学助教，负责大型人文学科讲座课程的讨论小组。这也意味着我要批改大量学生写作——而且，不可避免地，也会看到大量AI写作。当然，我们很多人都在努力设计作业和教学法，以降低这种诱惑。但作为助教，我实施这些政策的能力有限。与此同时，AI生成的写作如此普遍，以至于要认真对待课程政策，甚至把每一个疑似案例都上报给授课教授，那基本上每份作业都要提出几十次指控，其中一些还是误报。我相信人文学科教育具有神圣不可言喻的价值，但我也不会通过对每个人都在做的事情进行严厉打压，去说服那些压力重重的19岁学生相信这种价值。我该如何思考执行一个他们并不认真对待的机构的规则的伦理问题，或者为了营造一个不那么像需要绕过的障碍的课堂而放任自流？亲爱的烦恼的老师，我知道你说你相信“人文学科教育不可言喻的价值”，但如果我们想真正理清你的困境，那种不可言喻的价值必须被言说出来！那么：人文学科教育的真正价值是什么？放眼现代大学，人们可能会认为人文学科与STEM领域并无太大不同。正如工程系或数学系通过指出其创造的产品——桥梁设计、天气预报——来证明自身存在的合理性，如今的人文学科系也通过指出其学生同样创造产品来证明自身存在的合理性：文学解读。

##段落
翻译、文化批评、短片。但说真的：是大学的新自由主义化迫使人文科学陷入那种怪异的扭曲。那从来不是它们本该有的样子。正如哲学家梅根·弗里茨所写，它们的真正目标是“人的形成”。换句话说，虽然其他院系的目的最终是创造产品，但人文教育本该不同，因为学生本身就是产品。她才是学习过程中被创造和再创造的对象。填写这份匿名表格！订阅者将比其他人都更早看到我的专栏，他们的问题也会在未来的版本中被优先处理。在此注册！

##段落
这种教育愿景——作为一种旨在个人转变的追求——正是亚里士多德在古希腊时期提出的。他认为真正的目标不是传授知识，而是培养美德：诚实、正义、勇气，以及所有那些促成丰盈人生的性格特质。但由于在我们的超资本主义社会中，丰盈被贬低，你发现自己被困在最初的愿景和如今基于产品、功利主义的愿景之间。而学生们——正确地！——感觉到生成式AI证明了人文科学的功利主义愿景是个骗局。正如一位学生对他在纽约大学的教授所说，为了证明用AI帮他做作业的合理性：“你让我从A点到B点，我为什么不用车去呢？”这是一个完全合乎逻辑的论点——只要你接受功利主义的愿景。那么，真正的解决方案是对人文科学的目的保持诚实：你的事业是帮助学生培养他们的品格。我知道，我知道：很多学生会说：“我没时间培养品格！我只需要找到工作！”他们专注于就业前景完全合理。但你的工作是专注于别的东西——一些能帮助他们在长远中丰盈的东西，即使他们现在不完全看到它的价值。你的工作就是做他们的亚里士多德。

##段落
对于这位古希腊哲学家来说，所有美德之母是phronesis，即实践智慧。而我想说，你能为学生做的最有用的事，莫过于帮助他们培养这种美德，而AI的出现使它变得更重要，而不是更不重要。实践智慧超越了对一般规则的简单了解——比如“不要撒谎”——并像某种道德机器人那样机械地应用它们。它关乎在面对生活抛给你的复杂、动态情境时知道如何做出良好判断。有时那实际上意味着违背一条经典规则（在某些情况下，你应该撒谎！）。如果你已经

当你磨练了实践智慧，你将能够辨别特定情境中具有道德意义的关键特征，并给出与该情境高度契合的回应。这正是学生们步入更广阔世界时需要擅长的思考方式。技术创新的飞速步伐意味着他们将不得不一次又一次地选择如何利用新兴技术——以及如何不去利用。他们现在能获得的最佳训练，就是如何明智地做出这类选择。不幸的是，课堂上使用生成式AI恰恰可能会破坏这一点，因为它移除了一种极其宝贵的东西：摩擦。遭遇摩擦是我们锻炼认知肌肉的方式。将其从画面中移除，短期内会让事情变得更容易，但从长远来看，可能导致智力上的技能退化，我们的认知肌肉因缺乏使用而逐渐减弱。“实践智慧就像其他所有美德一样，通过实践来积累，所以如果你没有机会推理，也没有机会练习对某些事情进行深思，你以后就无法很好地深思，”技术哲学家香农·瓦洛去年告诉我。“我们需要大量认知锻炼来发展并保持实践智慧。有理由担心认知自动化会剥夺我们建立和保持这些认知肌肉的机会。”那么，你如何帮助学生保持并增强他们的实践智慧呢？通过尽可能多地给他们练习深思和选择的机会，将摩擦重新引入。如果我来设计课程，我不会采用严格的“禁止AI”政策。相反，我会对学生坦诚人文学科的真实益处，并解释为何盲目地利用AI作弊就是剥夺自己获得这种益处。然后，在写论文时，我会给他们两个选择：他们可以在AI帮助下写作，或者不依赖AI。两者完全可以。但如果他们确实从AI获得帮助，他们还必须写一篇课堂反思文章，解释为什么选择使用聊天机器人，以及他们认为这如何改变了他们的思维和学习过程。我会让它比原始作业更短，但比一段更长，这样迫使他们发展出他们试图避免使用的推理技能。作为助教，你可以向教授提出这个建议，但他们可能不会采纳。不幸的是，你在这里的自主权有限（除非你愿意冒险失去工作或离开它）。在这种情况下，你所能做的就是行使你确实拥有的自主权。所以，充分利用每一分。既然你带领讨论课，你处于有利位置来引导你的学生。

来锻炼他们在对话中的认知能力。你甚至可以组织一场关于AI的辩论：让一半学生为使用聊天机器人写论文辩护，另一半则反对。如果教授坚持严格的“禁止AI”政策，而你遇到明显由AI撰写的文章，你可能别无选择，只能举报。但如果某篇文章存在疑点，而学生在讨论中表现出非常深入的思考，你或许应倾向于宽容处理。至少这样你知道他们实现了最重要的目标。这一切都不容易。我对你以及所有在这个混乱环境中挣扎的教育者深表同情。事实上，如果有些教育者正遭受道德伤害——即当你感到被迫违背自身价值观时产生的心理状态——我也不会感到惊讶。但或许可以安慰你的是，记住这件事远非你一人所能左右。生成式AI对当前形式的人文学科教育构成了生存威胁。未来几年，人文学科部门必须经历范式转变，否则将消亡。如果他们想生存，就需要对自己真正的使命进行残酷的诚实审视。目前，从你处于范式转变前的视角来看，你所能做的只是做出留给你的选择。

我回想起了Shannon Vallor的第一本书《技术与美德：值得向往未来的哲学指南》。如果有一本书能让AI世界中的每个人都读到，那非它莫属。我认为它对其他人同样有益，因为我们都需培养Vallor所称的“技术道德美德”——这些特质能让我们很好地适应新兴技术。《纽约客》上一篇关于AI与认知萎缩的文章让我找到了一篇2024年的心理学论文，题为《思考的不愉快：心理努力与负面情绪关联的元分析综述》。作者的结论是：“我们建议，心理努力本质上令人厌恶。”再说一遍？是的，有时我只想关掉大脑看Netflix，但有时思考一个挑战性话题却如此愉快！对我来说，这就像跑步或举重：太多会令人疲惫，但适量则令人振奋。而“适量”的感觉会随着我的练习多少而上下波动。天体生物学家Sara Imari Walker在《Noema》杂志上发表了一篇题为《AI是生命》的文章，颇具挑衅性。她提醒我们，进化产生了我们，而我们产生了AI。“因此，它属于与生命起源同时出现的远古信息谱系的一部分，”她写道，“技术并非人为地替代生命——它就是生命。”需要明确的是，她并非主张技术是活的；她是在说技术是人类生命的延伸。

readings.title: Why you never really get over high school
body: 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laurie Clarke Popularity, one of the defining fixations of adolescence, seems to be seared into our consciousness for decades after we leave school. Before I was friends with Georgia*, I was scared of her.  One incident sticks in my mind. We were 14, and my best friend at the time was throwing a party – the kind that takes place in a rented church hall and where practically the whole school year turns up. But there was one group of people that my friend had neglected to invite. Georgia and her posse strode towards us across the playground, observers turning to stare. She was a terrifying bolt of fake tan, peroxide hair extensions and luminous sportswear – what could she possibly want with the likes of us? We froze as she came to a halt.  "We're invited to your party, yeah?" Georgia demanded of my friend. "Yes, of course," my friend managed to stutter back. Satisfied, Georgia turned on her heel and marched away. Another girl nearby murmured, "You don't have to invite them if you don't want to." But we all knew that yes, yes she did. You probably have similar high school recollections – of finding yourself at the sharp end of playground politics. Maybe you have memories of your own Georgia, a popular kid who could induce fear at a glance. Maybe you were a Georgia yourself. Either way, you probably remember it well. After speaking to hundreds of people about their experiences of high school, Mitch Prinstein, a professor of psychology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in the US, found that people's memories of those who once ruled over the school corridors – the queen bees, the prom kings, the star athletes – were remarkably potent. We're calling forth those experiences from when we were 14 to use as a kind of a template to see the world through – Mitch Prinstein Even decades after leaving school, most people are able to effortlessly recall the name of the most popular kid in their year – more so than the names of teachers and other classmates, wrote Prinstein ​i​n his 2017 book Popular: The Power of Likability in a Status-Obsessed World . And it's not just the memories that stick. We might be inclined to think that the high school hierarchy becomes irrelevant once we step beyond the school gates for the last time. But it turns out that it can exert a strange and persistent hold over us.  Research shows that how popular and well-liked we were as teenagers can influence our lives for years to come in everything from how we make sense of our social interactions to the strength of our romantic relations, our life satisfaction and even our health.  It was American psychologist John Coie who changed the way researchers thought about popularity.  His now-seminal studies in the early 1980s began by asking school kids two simple questions about their classmates: Who do you like the most? Who do you like the least? In the childish handwriting scrawled across hundreds of scraps of paper, Coie would trace new insights about human social behaviour.  You might think that children would be either broadly liked or disliked by their peers. In fact, Coie and his colleagues found kids can be both liked and disliked by different students, or neither liked nor disliked. Some children were named a lot by their peers – they were highly visible, like tiny celebrities. Others were barely mentioned at all. For the first time, Coie used the kids' answers to propose five social categories. "Accepted" and "rejected" for those who were widely liked or disliked respectively. "Controversial" for those who got a high number of both "likes" and "dislikes". "Neglected" for those who were hardly mentioned either way. And "average", for kids who weren't too extreme in any one direction (though most leaned towards one of the categories). Many studies have confirmed the usefulness of these labels. They generally find that about 40% of kids are "average" and 60% fit into one of the remaining four categories.  The most liked kids tend to be seen by their peers as kind, encouraging and supportive, while "neglecteds" tend to be quiet and withdrawn. "Rejected" kids are likely to be either aggressive and to bully others, or unassertive, socially anxious and the victims of bullying themselves . "Controversials", the rarest group, split the crowd – they're typically seen as class clowns or rebels. Remarkably, Coie found that children's labels largely stayed the same when they were introduced to new peer groups. And while the initial research was on primary school kids, many studies have replicated the findings in adolescents. One found that around half of kids maintain the same label they had at primary school five years later in high school.  "I'd had such a bad experience in primary school, and I always remember my mum saying 'It'll be better when you go to high school'," says Connie*, another friend I've asked about her high school experience. "But I think once you've been bullied, or if you have something that makes you visibly different… it was like I was easy pickings."  After being targeted by bullies in the first few months of high school, for reasons including being mixed race at a predominantly white institution, Connie switched schools. At her new school however, she soon encountered a similar pattern. (Read about the powerful new ways being discovered to fight bullying .) While the labels stay the same, the social dynamics shift dramatically between primary school and high school. In primary school, the "popular" kids are simply those who are best liked – often those who are well-behaved and excel at school, because at that point, kids values typically align with their adult supervisors. At high school, that changes . Adults and everything they stand for become woefully undesirable. A conscientious over-achiever might find themselves relegated to "nerd" status, while a rowdier, more divisive kid might find their star unexpectedly in ascendance. On the phone to the one-time playground terror and my now close friend Georgia, I ask her if she considered herself popular at high school. She tells me she didn't think of herself in this way. "'Popular' makes it sound as if people like you and I don't think we were necessarily liked," she says. "Maybe it was a bit more like, infamous… loud and attention-seeking." As a young teen, Georgia embodied the "controversial" archetype. She acted out aggressively and was disruptive in class. For all those who loved her, there were probably a fair few who didn't. I tell her that people, including myself, were pretty scared of her at one point. But she's wrong about this making her ineligible for the "popular" label.  "We start paying attention to who might be getting the most attention, who might be more dominant or 'cool'," says Prinstein. "Those who start becoming more physically attractive, those who are fitting into peer norms, [like] those who dress well or are good at sports."  Engaging in "pseudomature" behaviour – actions associated with older teens or adults – is another fast track to status. Teens who drink alcohol, take drugs and engage in precocious romantic behaviour are more likely to be considered popular – at least for a time. At around age 15, this behaviour stops conferring status to the same degree.  As high schoolers begin to mature, overt status-seeking becomes less socially expedient, and "likeability" begins to reassert itself as an important determinant of social standing. But the ripple effects from these early experiences in extreme social stratification can be consequential. "The experiences that we're having as kids – whether we're well liked, whether we're popular or high status – seem to have an enduring effect on us even 40 years later," says Prinstein. "Likability and status have pretty opposite effects. Likability is good. It generally leads to all kinds of positive health, work, academic and psychological outcomes.  "High status actually leads to the opposite ." Researchers used to think of high school culture as an immature version of adult society. In the 1960s, they began to understand that this "peer culture" was something much stranger – a parallel world animated by its own quixotic fascinations and sets of codes.  Rather than a simple hierarchy, the high school social landscape features a dynamic system of cliques. The key archetypes recur across popular culture, from American Pie to The Breakfast Club : the populars, the burnouts, the rejects and the nerds.  For the first few years of high school, the boundaries between cliques tend to be rigid. "Young people can become remarkably clannish, intolerant and cruel in their exclusion of others who are 'different'," wrote German-American psychoanalyst Erik Erikson in his 1959 book , Identity and the Life Cycle. It's a human phenomenon that some people achieve more social power and dominance over others. There's just something particularly acute about it in adolescence – Lucy Foulkes This intolerance, Erikson contended, might be "a necessary defence" against the loss of the identity one had as a child, combined with a mystifying onslaught of hormonal changes, and the overwhelming nature of the future, with all its possibilities and choices. Adolescents help each other through this discomfort "by forming cliques and stereotyping themselves", he suggested. This self-sorting makes it easier for teenagers to navigate their social worlds, because each person's relative "category" dictates how they should be treated.   One thing that is overlooked in popular culture, however, is the large swathe of teens who don't subscribe to any particular subculture. A 1985 study found that about 45% of highschoolers defined themselves simply as "normal". While the popular kids claimed they were all about looking good and partying, self-defined "normals" said things like "I'm just a regular teen". Being "abnormal" and standing out for the wrong reasons can be socially catastrophic. Connie remembers arriving at her new school aged 13 and finding it impossible to gain a foothold on the slippery social edifice. She describes her attempts to amplify different parts of herself in search of the right clique.   "I remember trying to be friends with the nerdy girls. I remember trying to be friends with the cool girls," she says. "I'd be like, 'Oh, I'm really bookish, I do all my homework.' And then that wasn't working, so it was like, 'Oh, I wear makeup, I do my hair,' that sort of thing. I tried to fit in with the music people. I started playing the trumpet."  But it was to no avail. "I think I knew in my heart that it just wasn't working," she says. "There was nowhere for me to slot in. By the end, I was just completely ignored by everyone."  Towards the end of high school, the punishing social hierarchy relaxes a little.  In the early 1990s, researcher David Kinney carried out an ethnographic research project where he embedded himself in a high school to observe the shifting boundaries of cliques up close. He tracked former "nerds" who managed to transition to "normals".  The rigidity of early high school cliques might reflect the limited cognitive capacities of young adolescents, he noted . While young teens are increasingly able to self-reflect, many are unable to differentiate between how often they think about themselves (a lot) and how often others do.  For many of the young "nerds" Kinney spoke to, this resulted in a debilitating self-focus and paralysis in social interactions. Eventually, continued cognitive development meant that former nerds were able to feel less fearful, and to surround themselves with peers who provided positive feedback. As teens mature, the strictures of conformity begin to loosen. Popular kids might even face threats from alternative, rebellious types. Kinney's study found that in later years, the "trendies" were challenged by students with "outrageous appearance and rowdy behaviour", who "competed with them for schoolwide popularity".  Some of these subtle shifts must have been underway when, aged 15, Georgia first asked me to hang out with her, but I still remember experiencing confusion and disbelief. At that point, I was a member of a predominantly male group of stoners. Was Georgia trying to play some kind of practical joke on me? Would I be lured out only to be humiliated in some way?   Almost 20 years later, I ask Georgia why she wanted to befriend me, something I've never asked her before. I'm wondering which of my sparkling attributes might have attracted her attention – my wit, my charm? "I guess there was a weirdness that we all shared," she says hesitantly. "Like, none of us were normal."  Given all its unique quirks, it’s remarkable how often we use high school as a frame of reference for adult interactions. When Lucy Foulkes, a psychologist at the University of Oxford in the UK and author of Coming of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Us , shared a social media post about the "mean girl" effect, she was met with an outpouring of recognition. "A lot of people were saying, it's not just teenagers, I see this in the workplace… I see this with mums at the school gate," says Foulkes. "It's a human phenomenon that some people achieve more social power and dominance over others. There's just something particularly acute about it in adolescence."  Foulkes points out that teens are surrounded by the same people almost every day for years in a way "that just doesn't really happen in adulthood, other than in the army or in prison. There is an intensity from the environment that goes beyond what's happening inside their brains." It's this intensity that partly explains why these experiences stay lodged within us, says Prinstein, shaping how we make sense of social encounters for years to come.  "We're calling forth those experiences from when we were 14 to use as a kind of a template to see the world through," says Prinstein. He points to studies suggesting that the mental model we use to process our social worlds begins to form in childhood , and that the memory-processing parts of the brain are active when people think about social behaviour . "Those memories are being brought back out all the time."  Many of us have likely wondered what happened to the "cool kids" we knew as teens. In a 2015 study , Joseph Allen, a professor of psychology at the University of Virginia in the US, sought to find out. His discoveries did not bode well for once-popular youths. Following 184 adolescents in the south-eastern US from ages 13 to 23, Allen found that status-hungry young people who engaged in pseudomature behaviour in their early teens were at greater risk of long-term difficulties in close relationships and criminal behaviour.  An early taste for alcohol and drugs was tied to greater vulnerability to substance abuse and addiction issues later in life. And a focus on status at an early age led to shallower bonds and difficulties sustaining friendships and romantic relationships.  The experience of being rejected can also leave scars. Prinstein's research found that rejected high school students were likely to become more depressed over time . He hypothesised that a negative feedback loop was at play, where the experience of rejection begets more withdrawal, which in turn intensifies feelings of rejection. People can absolutely turn it around. The problem is that we don't spend a lot of time talking about this – Mitch Prinstein By contrast, "likeability" – being "accepted" – in high school and generally, is one of the strongest predictors for positive life outcomes like a successful career , good health and strong relationships , even over and above factors like intelligence and socioeconomic background. Still, people who experience rejection can also develop important strengths, such as becoming more adept at identifying how others are feeling or being more aware of others being mistreated . Such emotional intelligence has been shown to be helpful in navigating personal relationships and the world of work .  And a child doesn't have to be "accepted" to enjoy a fulfilling social life as an adult. Studies have found that even just having one or two good friends as a teenager can confer a protective effect and strengthen future relationships.   Most importantly, it's within our power to change how our early experiences affect us. According to Prinstein, the high-school-honed social scripts we approach interactions with can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. "When we enter into a social context, we may be focusing on those pieces of information that confirm our worst expectations," he says. "Then we will behave in ways that might actually encourage more negative experiences." By choosing to update these frameworks – for example, deciding that a peer's ambiguous comment was probably not intended to upset us – we can help ourselves to have more rewarding experiences, he says.  As a reformed "high status" teen who engaged in risky, pseudomature behaviour from a young age, Georgia says, "I kind of have a sadness for my younger self, that I never got to experience just being a normal kid." She tells me that an early experience of seeing a friend beaten up, combined with abusive behaviour at home, convinced her to act aggressively to project invulnerability.  More like this: • The perks and pitfalls of laughing at yourself • How much of our personalities are determined at birth? • How I changed my personality in six weeks   She laments the fact that she didn't get more support at that age and was instead typecast by teachers as a "bad kid". "It's completely shaped my career trajectory and my fierce advocacy for vulnerable people," she says. Connie, meanwhile, says her early experiences of rejection eventually fed into a pattern of self-sabotage. "I think I'd given up on myself in a lot of ways, and I had so many self-destructive behaviours that it then became hard to maintain friendships," she says. This culminated in a period of crisis in her late adolescence, which she has since worked hard to heal from. More than a decade on, she has figured out what she loves – including a creative practice and a fulfilling career – and says she rarely thinks about her high school days.  Both Connie and Georgia are testament to the fact that the labels we once wore in high school don't have to be a life sentence.  "People can absolutely turn it around," Prinstein concurs. "The problem is that we don't spend a lot of time talking about this – meaning we are more likely to repeat our patterns."  * Names have been changed. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter   by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.
